name: Tara Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew of six for GreenShell, a retrofit firm. We take old 1960s terraces and low-rise council blocks and make them warm: new timber battens, external insulation, new windows, loft work. My morning starts with my phone, honestly. I photograph whatever wall we're on, an app turns it into a cut list, and I send the day's plan to the crew group in three languages, because Andrei reads Romanian best and Hodan prefers Somali. Then I'm up the scaffold with them till half four.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love seeing a family's heating bill drop. One lady on Ferry Lane told me she'd turned her heating off for the first time in October, and I nearly cried. What wears me out is that this is important work and it pays like it isn't. I'm the best on the crew and I'm on less than a warehouse supervisor, and GreenShell is about the only retrofit firm for fifty miles. I'm still paying off my van loan, so the account's empty most months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it was a good calculator, and the people who thought it would change everything got carried away. I'd still post about the apps I use, because they do make my day easier. Just not a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit disappointed. I'd hoped it might take the boring parts off us and leave the good bits. If it stalls, I'm still on low pay doing the paperwork at night, just a little faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going with what I'm doing. I'd keep testing every new app that comes out, because even a small saving matters on a crew of six. And I'd keep pushing GreenShell's boss to let the crew share in the time we save, like an early Friday finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly flat, maybe, like a film that had a good trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a bit disappointed. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can see what it could do for us. Picture a robot doing the dull, dangerous bit, drilling a thousand fixings into concrete, while we do the fiddly work round windows. That's a better job. If it fizzles, we just keep wrecking our shoulders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what does the next couple of years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same crew, same blocks, same van loan. I'd maybe have it paid off in eighteen months and finally start saving. Jonas and I keep saying we'll go somewhere warm one summer, and we'd keep saying it.

S0.say: I'd say it was a good calculator, and the people who thought it would change everything got carried away. I'd still share the apps that make my day easier.
S0.think: I'm a bit disappointed, because I hoped it would take the boring parts off us. If it stalls, I'm still on low pay doing paperwork at night, just faster.
S0.do: Keeps leading her crew and testing every new app for small time savings. Pushes her boss to let the crew share saved time, for example with an early Friday finish.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a film that had a good trailer.
S0.quote: If it fizzles, we just keep wrecking our shoulders.
S0.fieldNote: Tara is the rare worker who would be let down if AI stalled. She wants machines to take the dangerous, dull work so people keep the skilled parts. Her money is tight because of a van loan, but she frames that as temporary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, but only if workers get a say in how it's used. I'd post about it, I'd bring it up at the union, and I'd tell the crew to get their hands on every new tool before the managers decide for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. I'm already the one on site who sorts out the apps, so I'd be the one they ask to run the new kit. The danger is for the people who don't get the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask GreenShell straight away to send me on any robot or scanner training going, and I'd do online courses at night on building energy assessments. I'd set up a little group with the crew where we share what works, in all three languages. And I'd push the union to get a written agreement on retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, actually a bit excited. I'd feel like I was in the right place for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides who gets the good new jobs on your site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, the boss, and he picks whoever he likes. That's why I'd want it written down in a union agreement. Otherwise it's Andrei and Hodan who get left out, because their English isn't great, and they're two of my best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the money from the savings all goes upwards, yes. I could be running three robots and still be on the same low wage. That's the part I'd fight about.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance, but only if workers get a say in how it's used. I'd tell the crew to get hold of every new tool before managers decide for them.
S1.think: It's probably good for me, because I'm already the one who sorts out the apps and I'd be asked to run new kit. The danger is for those who don't get the chance.
S1.do: Asks her employer for robot and scanner training straight away and studies building energy assessment online at night. Sets up a multilingual tool-sharing group with her crew and pushes for a union retraining agreement.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a bit excited, as if she were in the right place for once.
S1.quote: I could be running three robots and still be on the same low wage.
S1.fieldNote: Tara expects to do well personally and quickly turns to who gets left behind, naming two crew members by language. Her worry is not the technology but who keeps the savings. She would act within weeks, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any of us to be blamed for not keeping up. The government has to step in with income support, and the firms making these machines should pay for it. I'd say that everywhere, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good with the apps doesn't save me if the app can do the whole job. In two years, the skills I've been proud of picking up early get overtaken too. I'd be running to stand still with no money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the boss and offer to be the one who runs and maintains the robots, because someone has to, at least at first. I'd cut back to nothing, sell my good camera, put off the van upgrade. And I'd help organise the crew to demand that any savings from the robots pay for proper redundancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm used to being ahead, and two years would leave me no chance to get ahead of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the crew. What would you tell them the week it's announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit them down in the cabin and tell them straight, this is coming, nobody here did anything wrong, and we stick together. Then I'd help each of them write a CV, using the AI, which is a bit of a bad joke really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money scares you more than the robots. Explain that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn a robot in a week. What I can't do is go three months without pay while I find the next thing. That's the bit that's out of my hands. Change is fine, being broke during it isn't.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to be blamed for not keeping up. The government has to step in with income support, paid for by the firms making these machines.
S2.think: Being good with the apps doesn't save me if the app can do the whole job. In two years my early-adopter skills get overtaken too, and I'd have no money in the bank.
S2.do: Offers to run and maintain the first robots at her firm. Cuts spending hard, sells her good camera and delays the van upgrade, and organises the crew to demand proper redundancy pay from the savings.
S2.feel: Alarmed, because for once she would have no chance to get ahead.
S2.quote: I can learn a robot in a week. What I can't do is go three months without pay while I find the next thing.
S2.fieldNote: This is the key tension for Tara: her adaptability is real, but her thin cushion is the limit. She would still move first and take on the robots, while organising her crew. The joke about writing CVs with AI showed she sees the irony.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set things up properly if we start now. I'd be talking about worker-owned firms, where the crew owns the machines, not some investor. I'd probably write long posts about it that nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is the sweet spot for me. Long enough to learn and save a bit, short enough that I'd take it seriously and not drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the energy assessor qualification in the first year and start doing assessments at weekends for extra money, maybe a couple a month. I'd save every bit of that. And with Andrei and two others, I'd start planning a small retrofit co-op that owns a robot or two and does the jobs GreenShell won't touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the useful kind. It would push me rather than freeze me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the co-op look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four or five of us, equal shares, small jobs on older houses. We'd hire the robots for the heavy drilling and do the careful work ourselves. Whatever the machines save, we keep, not a boss two towns away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Jonas feel about you putting money into that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be nervous. He fixes bikes, he's careful with money, more careful than me. But I'd show him the numbers, and I'd promise not to touch the rent money. He'd come round, he usually does when there's a plan on paper.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to set things up properly if we start now. I'd be talking about worker-owned firms where the crew owns the machines, not an investor.
S3.think: Five years is the sweet spot for me: long enough to learn and save, short enough that I'd take it seriously and not drift.
S3.do: Finishes an energy assessor qualification in the first year and does a couple of weekend assessments a month for extra income, saving it all. Plans a small retrofit co-op with three colleagues that would own a robot or two.
S3.feel: Anxious in a useful way that pushes her rather than freezing her.
S3.quote: Whatever the machines save, we keep, not a boss two towns away.
S3.fieldNote: Given a few years, Tara's progressive views turn into a concrete plan: a worker co-op owning the machines. She is realistic about her partner's caution and about money. Five years is the timeline that suits her best, by her own account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade, so let's use it to make sure the robots are owned by communities and workers, not just a few companies. I'd join any campaign for that, and I'd say it at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly safe. I'm young, I like new things, and ten years is enough to retrain twice if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same things as before but slower: energy assessor course, weekend assessments, saving. Maybe in year four or five, try the co-op once we'd seen how the robots really perform on jobs. I'd want the van paid off first, and some savings, so I'm not betting the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. It's a big change at the end, but there's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd get comfortable with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Definitely. Ten years is long enough to tell yourself next year. That's why I'd set dates, like co-op talks by year three, or I know I'd keep putting it off with a full diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven when it arrives. Where do you hope to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a small co-op with a couple of robots and four or five people, doing retrofits nobody else wants. Earning a bit more than now. Maybe Jonas and I would finally have taken that summer holiday.

S4.say: I'd say we have a decade, so let's make sure the robots are owned by communities and workers, not a few companies. I'd join any campaign for that.
S4.think: I'd feel fairly safe. I'm young, I like new things, and ten years is enough to retrain twice if I need to.
S4.do: Follows the same plan more slowly, studying energy assessment and doing weekend jobs while saving. Pays off the van first, then sets dates to start the co-op around year four or five once the robots have proved themselves.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with a big change at the end but room to breathe.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to tell yourself next year.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Tara slows down but sets herself deadlines because she knows time can breed drift. She would not bet the rent, which shows her thin cushion still shapes risk even for an adaptive person. She keeps the collective goal of workers owning machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I couldn't learn, but because I'd have no money to live on while I did. What would help is income support that kicks in while you retrain, not after you've already lost the flat, and some way for workers to own a share of the machines that replace them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who don't speak the language well. Half my crew are brilliant builders and would struggle with an online course in English. Any help has to work for them too, or it's not help.

headlineQuote: Change is fine, being broke during it isn't.
portrait: Tara is a 27-year-old crew lead for a retrofit firm, insulating old council housing, who uses AI apps every day and runs her crew's plans in three languages. She lives with her partner Jonas, a careful bike mechanic, and has almost no savings while she pays off a van loan. She is calm, even excited, in the slower pictures, because she expects to be the one running the new machines, but alarmed at AGI in two years because her empty account leaves no room to retrain. Over five or ten years she plans an energy assessor qualification and a small worker co-op that owns its own robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, not because she couldn't learn, but because she'd have no money to live on while she did.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that starts while people retrain, a way for workers to own a share of the machines, and help that works for people who struggle with English.
